drills.q: What does assign y = a & b; describe?
options: A permanent connection between y and an AND gate fed by a and b
A computation that runs once when the module is elaborated
A computation that runs every time a or b changes
A value copied into y at the next clock edge
drills.why: The verb is not compute, it is is. The connection is as true a nanosecond from now as it was a year ago, and if a changes then y changes because the wire is still there.

drills.q: Does the order of continuous assignments in a module matter?
options: No, because a circuit has no first line
Yes, a signal must be driven before it is read
Yes, but only for signals that cross module boundaries
Only in simulation, not in synthesis
drills.why: A signal is a node, not a variable that acquires a value at some moment. Reorder every continuous assignment in a module and the synthesised hardware is identical.

drills.q: What happens when two continuous assignments drive the same wire?
options: It is an error, because it describes two gate outputs soldered together
The later one wins, as it would in a program
The tool builds a multiplexer and picks at random
The wire takes the or of the two values
drills.why: Nothing about the second line replaces the first, because there is no first. Both connections exist at once, which is the same short circuit the tri-state buffer exists to prevent on a shared bus.

drills.q: What does a synthesiser do after mapping a design onto cells?
options: Deletes anything whose value cannot change and anything nothing reads
Places and routes the cells onto a floorplan
Verifies the design against a testbench
Inserts flip-flops wherever a path is too slow
drills.why: That is the step people are not ready for. It is also why a cell count is the answer to a better question than "what did I type": it says how much hardware you actually asked for.

drills.q: How many gates does assign y = a & 1'b1; produce?
options: None, the output is a and a wire is cheaper than a gate
One AND gate, as written
One buffer cell, to drive the output
It depends on whether a is an input or an internal wire
drills.why: The optimiser folds the constant away. This is also why a design can silently be smaller than intended: an unused output is deleted with exactly the same enthusiasm.

drills.q: What is in the hardware after a for loop with four iterations is synthesised?
options: Four copies of the body, side by side, all settling together
A counter and one copy of the body
One copy of the body, evaluated four times per clock
A state machine with four states
drills.why: The tool unrolls the loop while elaborating. There is no thing that goes around four times, and there is no counter anywhere in the result.

drills.q: Why must a loop bound be known at build time?
options: It decides how many copies of the body exist, and silicon cannot change how much of itself there is
The simulator needs it to schedule events
Otherwise the loop cannot be proved to terminate
It does not have to be, the tool infers a maximum
drills.why: A loop whose count depends on an input would need the amount of hardware to change while the chip is running.

drills.q: In software a loop is cheap and the body is what you pay for. What changes here?
options: The loop is the multiplier: four iterations is four copies in area and power
Nothing, the cost model is the same
The body is free and the loop costs a counter
Cost depends only on the clock frequency
drills.why: This is the first real difference between describing hardware and writing software, and it reorganises how you think about what an expression costs.

drills.q: What does instantiating a module twice give you?
options: Two separate pieces of the chip that share only a description
One piece of hardware used twice
Two calls to the same logic, resolved at elaboration
A single instance, since the tool deduplicates identical modules
drills.why: There is no stack, nothing returns, and nothing is reused between the instances. A module you instantiate a thousand times costs a thousand times as much.

drills.q: How do you make two uses share one piece of hardware?
options: Build it on purpose, with a multiplexer to choose the inputs and a register to hold the result
Instantiate the module once and read its output twice
Mark the module as shared and let the tool schedule it
Put both uses inside the same always block
drills.why: It is never free and never automatic. It also takes more than one clock cycle, which is the trade Part V spends most of its time on.

drills.q: What does a delay like #5 mean to a synthesiser?
options: Nothing, it is ignored
It inserts a five gate delay buffer chain
It constrains the path to five nanoseconds
It is a syntax error outside a testbench
drills.why: It is meaningful to the simulator, which has a notion of time, and invisible to the tool that builds structure. That gap has a name: simulation and synthesis mismatch.

drills.q: What is a simulation and synthesis mismatch?
options: A design that passes every test and behaves differently as a chip
A design that synthesises but cannot be simulated
A timing violation found after place and route
A disagreement between two synthesis tools
drills.why: The same text is read by two tools with different jobs. Most of the language means the same thing to both, and a subset does not.

drills.q: Why is a five-bit sum assigned through a four-bit intermediate wrong?
options: The addition happens at four bits, so the carry is gone before the widening
The intermediate wire adds a gate delay that breaks the timing
Assigning a narrow wire to a wide one sign extends instead of zero extending
It is not wrong, the tool widens the operands automatically
drills.why: Width is decided where an expression is evaluated, not where its result eventually lands. Widening afterwards cannot recover a bit that was already dropped.

drills.q: Why did the drawn schematic have to be replaced by text?
options: A real design has millions of gates and nobody draws millions of anything
Text can be version controlled and a drawing cannot
Schematics cannot express sequential logic
Foundries stopped accepting schematic submissions
drills.why: Drawing works up to a few hundred gates, which is where Part II stopped. The description that replaces it looks like a program, and every hour lost in this part is lost to that resemblance.

drills.q: Which report should you trust about what your design contains?
options: The tool's, because it has already deleted everything you asked for by accident
Your reading of the source, because it says what you intended
The simulator's, because it executes the real behaviour
Neither, until the design is placed and routed
drills.why: The gap between what you wrote and what survives is where most of the surprise in this part lives.
